You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose exactly 1 design.
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 2 of 24.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out, min} \ge 1.8 \text{ V}$
        *   $V_{out, max} \le 3.6 \text{ V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05 \text{ V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4 \text{ s}$
        *   $dv \le 0.02 \text{ V}$ (settling)
    *   Previous Design (SSHI_FBR_Clamp):
        *   Structure: Full bridge rectifier + an L-S (inductor-switch) SSHI-like circuit + Zener clamp + storage capacitor.
        *   Results:
            *   $V_{avg}$ is generally okay (often $> 1.8 \text{ V}$).
            *   $V_{max}$ is okay (capped by Zener at 3.3V).
            *   $V_{pp}$ (ripple) is too high (up to 345 mV).
            *   $t_{up}$ (startup) is failing on S4 (0.52 s).
            *   $dv$ (settled) is failing across almost all conditions (significant drift).
    *   Diagnosis provided:
        *   Startup too slow on S4: Storage capacitor $C_1$ might be too large, or power delivery at low voltage is too low.
        *   Output drifting ($dv$): Storage time constant $\tau = R_L C_{out}$ is too long.
        *   Ripple ($V_{pp}$) too high: Storage capacitor $C_{out}$ is too small to buffer the pulses.

    Wait, the diagnosis is contradictory.
    - "Storage time constant is too long" $\rightarrow$ Decrease $C_{out}$.
    - "Storage cannot buffer charge pulses" $\rightarrow$ Increase $C_{out}$.
    - "Startup is too slow" $\rightarrow$ Decrease $C_{out}$ (or increase current).

    Let's re-examine the physics:
    The ripple $V_{pp}$ is caused by the pulsed nature of the SSHI circuit. In a standard FBR, the ripple is lower because the charging is more continuous. In SSHI, we get high-current spikes.
    $V_{pp} \approx \frac{\Delta Q}{C_{out}}$. To reduce $V_{pp}$, we need a larger $C_{out}$.
    However, $dv = |V_{avg}(0.7-0.8) - V_{avg}(0.6-0.7)|$. If $C_{out}$ is very large, the voltage takes a long time to reach steady state. If the time constant $\tau = R_L C_{out}$ is too large, $V_{out}$ will still be climbing (or falling) at $t=0.8 \text{ s}$, leading to a large $dv$.
    $t_{up}$ is the time to reach $1.8 \text{ V}$. If $C_{out}$ is too large, it takes longer to charge from $0 \text{ V}$ to $1.8 \text{ V}$.

    So, the conflict is:
    $C_{out} \uparrow \implies V_{pp} \downarrow$ (Good) but $t_{up} \uparrow$ (Bad) and $dv \uparrow$ (Bad).
    $C_{out} \downarrow \implies V_{pp} \uparrow$ (Bad) but $t_{up} \downarrow$ (Good) and $dv \downarrow$ (Good).

    We need to find a balance or change the circuit to reduce the ripple without relying solely on a massive $C_{out}$.

    The current SSHI-FBR implementation:
    - FBR: D1-D4.
    - L-S combination: L1 and S1.
    - Zener: DZ1.
    - Cap: C1.

    Wait, is the current "SSHI" topology correct?
    `L1: pzp -> n1`, `S1: n1 -> pzn`.
    When S1 closes, L1 is in parallel with the piezo (pzp-pzn). This is the standard SSHI inversion step.
    The current flows through the rectifier D1-D4.

    Wait, looking at the components:
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    L1: pzp -> n1
    S1: n1 -> pzn

    This is a rectifier with an inductor-switch inverter.
    The inversion occurs when S1 closes, flipping the voltage across $C_p$.
    However, if the ripple is too high, it might be because the charge is delivered in large, infrequent bursts.

    Can we improve the ripple without just changing $C_{out}$?
    A full-bridge rectifier (FBR) alone had $V_{pp} = 26.2 \text{ mV}$ (ok), but it failed $V_{avg}$ on S2/S4 and $V_{max}$ on S3.
    The SSHI-FBR improved the power (higher $V_{avg}$) but introduced ripple.

    Let's look at the rectifier again. A full bridge is used. Is there a way to smooth the output more efficiently?
    Or perhaps the "SSHI" part can be modified.
    Standard SSHI usually has a flying capacitor $C_{fly}$ instead of just an inductor. Inductive SSHI is possible.

    Wait, the problem says "storage cannot buffer the charge pulses against the load".
    If $C_{out}$ is too small, $V_{pp}$ is high.
    If $C_{out}$ is too large, $t_{up}$ and $dv$ are bad.

    Maybe we can use a different rectifier or a different SSHI approach.
    What if we use a half-bridge? No, we need the full swing.
    What if we use a different inductor placement?
    Or maybe we use a smaller $L$ to change the pulse characteristics? (Though values are tuned automatically).

    Let's consider the "settled" failure.
    S1: $dv = 75 \text{ mV}$.
    S2: $dv = 230 \text{ mV}$.
    S4: $dv = 313 \text{ mV}$.
    These are quite high. $C_{out} = 4.7 \mu\text{F}$.
    For S4, $R_L = 1 \text{ M}\Omega$. $\tau = R_L C_{out} = 10^6 \times 4.7 \times 10^{-6} = 4.7 \text{ s}$.
    Wait! $\tau = 4.7 \text{ seconds}$ is huge compared to the simulation time of $0.8 \text{ s}$.
    No wonder $dv$ is failing. The capacitor is still charging linearly.
    To get $dv \le 0.02 \text{ V}$ at $t=0.7-0.8 \text{ s}$, we need the time constant to be much smaller, or the system to have reached steady state.
    For $\tau = R_L C_{out}$, we typically need $t \approx 3 \tau$ to $5 \tau$ to settle.
    $0.8 \text{ s} / 5 \approx 0.16 \text{ s}$.
    So $R_L C_{out}$ should be around $0.16 \text{ s}$.
    For $R_L = 1 \text{ M}\Omega$, $C_{out} \approx 0.16 / 10^6 = 160 \text{ nF}$.
    But for $R_L = 150 \text{ k}\Omega$ (S2), $C_{out}$ could be larger.
    However, for S4, $C_{out} = 4.7 \mu\text{F}$ is way too large.

    Wait, if I reduce $C_{out}$ to $1 \mu\text{F}$ or less:
    - $t_{up}$ improves (faster charge).
    - $dv$ improves (faster settling).
    - $V_{pp}$ increases (more ripple).

    Is there a way to reduce ripple without a huge $C_{out}$?
    The ripple is $V_{pp}$. For the SSHI circuit, the energy is delivered in bursts twice per period ($f=100 \text{ Hz}, T=10 \text{ ms}$).
    If we can deliver the charge more continuously, $V_{pp}$ will drop.
    But the SSHI inversion is inherently a pulsed event.

    Wait, looking at the FBR reference:
    S1: $V_{pp} = 26.2 \text{ mV}, C_{out} = 2.2 \mu\text{F}$.
    The FBR has much lower ripple because it charges the capacitor every half-cycle with a smoother current (limited by $C_p$ and $R_{load}$).
    The SSHI-FBR creates high-current spikes because of the $L C_p$ resonance.

    Could we use a different topology?
    Maybe a Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) circuit?
    SECE uses a switch to connect $C_p$ to a rectifier.
    In SECE, the charge is extracted at the peaks of $V_{pzp}$.
    Let's try a SECE-like structure.
    SECE Topology:
    - Piezo $C_p$ is connected to a switch.
    - The switch connects to a rectifier (half-bridge or full-bridge) which then charges $C_{out}$.
    Actually, a simpler SECE is:
    `S1` connects `pzp` to `n1` (where `n1` is the input to a rectifier).
    But we have a piezo with `pzp` and `pzn`.
    A common SECE:
    - $S_1$ connects `pzp` to `rect_in`.
    - $S_2$ connects `pzn` to `rect_in`.
    But we only have 2 SYNCs and 4 switches.

    Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" or a simple SSHI with a smaller $C_{out}$ and see if the tuning can fix it.
    Wait, the problem is the $C_{out}$ trade-off.
    Is there any other way to reduce ripple?
    Maybe a small LC filter at the output?
    $L_{filter}$ between the rectifier and $C_{out}$.
    This would block the high-frequency spikes from the SSHI pulses.
    Current path: `Rectifier` $\rightarrow$ `L_filter` $\rightarrow$ `C_out` $\rightarrow$ `R_load`.
    This is a $\pi$-filter or a simple LC low-pass.

    Let's try:
    - Maintain the SSHI-FBR topology for high power.
    - Add an inductor $L_{filter}$ between the bridge output and $C_{out}$.
    Wait, the bridge output is node `out`. If I put $L_{filter}$ there, I need a new node.
    `Bridge` $\rightarrow$ `n_filt` $\rightarrow$ `L_filter` $\rightarrow$ `out` $\rightarrow$ `C_out` $\rightarrow$ `0`.
    This would smooth the current entering $C_{out}$.

    Let's refine this:
    D1: pzp -> n_filt
    D2: pzn -> n_filt
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    L1: pzp -> n1 (SSHI)
    S1: n1 -> pzn (SSHI)
    G1: SYNC
    L2: n_filt -> out (Filter)
    C1: out -> 0 (Storage)
    DZ1: 0 -> out (Clamp)

    Wait, does the Zener clamp still work? Yes, it's at the output.
    Does the filter inductor $L_2$ interfere with the Zener? Not really.
    Would $L_2$ slow down the startup? Yes, but probably less than a huge $C_{out}$ would.
    Would it increase $V_{pp}$? No, it should decrease it.

    Let's check the component count:
    D1, D2, D3, D4 (4)
    L1, S1, G1 (3)
    L2 (1)
    C1 (1)
    DZ1 (1)
    Total = 10 components. (Limit is 16).

    Wait, the rectifier in the previous design was:
    D1: pzp -> out
    D2: pzn -> out
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    This is a full bridge.
    Wait, the "return" diodes D3, D4 are connected to ground.
    The current flow is:
    Positive half: pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow$ D4 $\rightarrow$ pzn.
    Negative half: pzn $\rightarrow$ D2 $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow$ D3 $\rightarrow$ pzp.
    This is correct.

    Now, if I add $L_2$:
    D1: pzp -> n_filt
    D2: pzn -> n_filt
    D3: 0 -> pzp
    D4: 0 -> pzn
    L2: n_filt -> out
    C1: out -> 0
    L1, S1, G1 as before.

    One problem: In the positive half-cycle, the current flows pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ n_filt $\rightarrow$ L2 $\rightarrow$ out $\rightarrow$ RL $\rightarrow$ 0 $\rightarrow$ D4 $\rightarrow$ pzn.
    This is still a complete loop. The L2 inductor will smooth the current charging $C_{out}$.

    Wait, I need to make sure the startup $t_{up}$ is not too slow. $L_2$ might add some impedance, but for $u\text{A}$ currents, it's negligible unless $L_2$ is huge.
    The main benefit is that we can now use a *smaller* $C_{out}$ to satisfy $t_{up}$ and $dv$, while the $L_2 C_{out}$ filter handles the ripple $V_{pp}$.

    Let's check the $L_2$ value. A few mH should be enough to filter $100\text{ Hz}$ pulses if $C_{out}$ is in the $\mu\text{F}$ range.
    $f_{cutoff} = 1 / (2 \pi \sqrt{L_2 C_{out}})$.
    If $L_2 = 10 \text{ mH}$ and $C_{out} = 1 \mu\text{F}$, $f_{cutoff} \approx 1.6 \text{ kHz}$.
    The SSHI pulses are much faster (ton $\approx 34 \mu\text{s}$), so this filter will be very effective.

    Let's double-check the "settled" requirement again.
    For S4, $R_L = 1 \text{ M}\Omega$.
    If $C_{out} = 1 \mu\text{F}$, $\tau = 1 \text{ s}$. Still potentially too slow?
    Wait, $0.8 \text{ s}$ is the total time. $dv$ is measured between $0.6-0.7 \text{ s}$ and $0.7-0.8 \text{ s}$.
    If $\tau = 1 \text{ s}$, the voltage $V(t) = V_{final}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$.
    $V(0.65) = V_f(1 - e^{-0.65}) = 0.478 V_f$.
    $V(0.75) = V_f(1 - e^{-0.75}) = 0.527 V_f$.
    $dv = 0.049 V_f$.
    If $V_f = 2.5 \text{ V}$, $dv = 0.12 \text{ V}$. Still $> 0.02 \text{ V}$.
    So for S4, we might need $C_{out}$ even smaller, say $220 \text{ nF}$.
    $\tau = 1 \text{ M}\Omega \times 220 \text{ nF} = 0.22 \text{ s}$.
    $V(0.65) = V_f(1 - e^{-0.65/0.22}) = V_f(1 - 0.05) = 0.95 V_f$.
    $V(0.75) = V_f(1 - e^{-0.75/0.22}) = V_f(1 - 0.03) = 0.97 V_f$.
    $dv = 0.02 V_f$.
    If $V_f = 2.5 \text{ V}$, $dv = 0.05 \text{ V}$. Still a bit high, but much closer.
